lines.narration: On the morning of their fifth anniversary, Amy Dunne walked out of her house and never came back.
The investigation that follows will tear her husband's life apart - and the truth, when it comes, will be worse than anyone could imagine.
How well do you really know the person sleeping next to you?
I'm Serabudabu, and today we're diving into Gone Girl, twenty-fourteen. A psychological thriller where every clue is a lie, and the truth comes at a cost.
It opens on Amy, while Nick's voice circles the questions a marriage never stops asking. What are you thinking. How are you feeling. What have we done to each other.
That morning he stops by the bar he runs with his twin sister, Margo. It is his fifth anniversary, and he sits there restless and flat, a man who would rather be anywhere else.
In flashback we see how it began. Nick and Amy meet at a New York party, trading clever lines, each convinced they have found the one person sharp enough to keep up.
For a while, they really are that couple. But the charm that pulls them together is also a performance, and neither of them will be able to keep it up forever.
Back in the present, Nick returns home to find the front door open and signs of a struggle inside.
He calls the police. Detective Boney and Officer Gilpin arrive and walk the house.
Something about the scene bothers them. It looks less like a break-in than like a picture of one, as if someone wanted it to be found.
Amy, it turns out, is a kind of celebrity. Her parents wrote a beloved children's series, Amazing Amy, modeled on their own daughter.
But the fictional Amazing Amy was always one polished step better than the real girl. Amy has spent her whole life measured against a perfect version of herself, and quietly losing.
In his first interview, Nick fumbles the simplest questions about his wife. He cannot name her friends, or say how she spends her days, or even recall her blood type.
To the detectives, that distance looks like guilt. What it really shows is a husband who stopped paying attention to his own wife.
The detectives turn up an old boyfriend, Desi Collings, a wealthy man who once stalked Amy and never quite let go of her.
And in Amy's study they find the first clue of one of her anniversary treasure hunts. Every year she hid a trail of riddles for Nick to solve. This year, the police want to follow it too.
Amy's diary fills in the years between. It tells us of a couple who promised never to turn bitter.
Then the recession takes their jobs and the money runs thin. And according to her account, the marriage slowly curdles into resentment.
For Amy, the diary suggests, this was never only about money. Without the life they built in New York, the Nick she fell for seems to disappear, and so does the marriage she had pinned herself to.
As the town searches for the missing woman, the pressure begins to settle onto her husband.
A candlelight vigil gathers for the missing Amy. The whole town turns out, and Nick stands before the cameras to plead for his wife's safe return.
Then a friend steps forward with news that stuns the room. Amy, she says, was six weeks pregnant when she vanished.
Nick insists he never knew about any baby. But to the watching police, and the millions following the case, his shock looks a great deal like guilt.
The evidence keeps pointing inward. A scene that looks staged. Blood mopped up in the kitchen. Hidden debt, and a life insurance policy quietly raised in Amy's name months before she vanished.
Then the detectives uncover the last piece. Nick has been having an affair with one of his young students. A pregnant wife, a secret girlfriend, and a fortune in insurance. Now he has a motive.
Everything says Nick killed his wife. Everything, that is, except the one fact the police do not have yet.
Because Amy is alive. We find her driving down a country road, watching her own disappearance unfold on the radio.
She was never taken. She planned all of it. The grieving wife was a performance, and Nick is being framed for a murder that never happened.
In her telling, she shows us how it was done. She befriended a pregnant neighbor and stole her urine to fake the pregnancy.
She staged the house the morning Nick left, building a crime scene with just enough mistakes to raise doubt.
She made herself bleed, then cleaned it up badly, the way a panicking husband would.
And she wrote a diary, hundreds of entries inventing the abuse and the fear, burned just enough to be found.
Then she explains the marriage itself. For years she played the Cool Girl Nick wanted, the easygoing woman who liked everything he liked and never complained.

And that is the real horror underneath the kidnapping. The Amy that Nick loved was a role, and the resentment beneath it had been building for years. When he grew lazy and unfaithful, she decided he would not get to win.
Nick and Margo work through the treasure-hunt clues and realize the truth. Amy is framing him for her own murder.
Amy, meanwhile, disappears into a backwoods motel under a new name, dyed hair, plain glasses, waiting for the story to do its work.
Cornered by the case against him, Nick hires Tanner Bolt, a lawyer who specializes in men everyone already believes are guilty.
On the news, Nick is convicted in the court of public opinion, a wife-killer in every headline.
But Amy's perfect plan has a weakness she did not see coming. At the motel, a neighbor spots the cash she is carrying.
That night the couple turns on her, demanding the money and refusing to take no for an answer.
They take nearly everything. Broke and exposed, Amy, who controlled every detail, is suddenly out of options.
So she calls the one man who would still take her in without question. Her old admirer Desi, who never stopped loving the girl who got away.
Desi installs her in his secluded lake house, a place of every comfort, with cameras watching every door and window.
But his devotion comes with conditions. The more he gives, the more he expects, and the refuge becomes another cage. Amy has traded a husband who ignored her for a man who will never let her go.
Back home, Nick makes a move of his own. He sits for a televised interview with Sharon Schieber.
On camera he confesses the affair and performs his remorse, saying exactly what the audience needs to hear.
At the lake house, Amy watches, and for the first time she sees her husband doing the one thing she does best. He is performing, and he is good at it.
Boney, still unconvinced by the tidy case, keeps pulling at the evidence that does not fit.
Watching Nick win the public back, Amy makes her decision. She wants to go home. But to do that, she has to get free of Desi, and she has only one way out.
She draws him close one last night, playing the grateful, devoted woman he always wanted.
Then she kills Desi, and arranges the scene so it will read as a woman escaping a captor.
She leaves the room exactly as she needs it, turned into evidence for the story she is about to sell.
Covered in blood, she drives back through the night toward the life she walked away from.
And Amy returns, collapsing into Nick's arms before a wall of cameras, the missing wife miraculously, impossibly home.
At the hospital she gives the police a careful, tearful account, casting Desi as the obsessed kidnapper who held and assaulted her for weeks.
Boney does not believe a word of it. She keeps asking how a captive tied up for weeks got hold of a box cutter. But the story is airtight, and the public wants its miracle.
Alone with Nick, Amy drops the act and tells him the truth. She murdered Desi, and came home for the husband who finally understands exactly what she is capable of.

And the pregnancy that was a lie at the vigil is suddenly real, made true with sperm Nick stored years before. She uses the coming child as a lock on the door. If he leaves, he leaves his baby. Nick is trapped.
And so they stay together. They announce the coming baby and settle in as the perfect couple, smiling for the cameras. Nick holds Amy's secrets, and Amy holds his, and neither one can ever let go.

Gone Girl is a story about marriage as performance, and the terrifying idea that the people who know us best are the ones who can destroy us. In the end, Nick and Amy deserve each other. Thanks for watching. If you enjoyed this dive, hit like and subscribe for more. See you in the next one.
